content.intro: Generic Interfaces and Delegates is lesson 98 in Generics and Type-Safe Reuse. Polymorphism lets callers use a stable contract while implementations vary. Use inheritance for a genuine subtype relationship and composition when objects collaborate.
content.why_it_matters: Generics avoid duplicating algorithms while preserving useful information about the values being processed. This lesson focuses on generic interfaces and delegates and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for generic interfaces and delegates. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Generic interfaces
items.text: Generics preserve type information while letting one implementation work with many types. Constraints state requirements at compile time; variance changes assignment compatibility only in supported input/output positions.

items.title: Generic delegates
items.text: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a callable method or function. Func, Action, and Predicate cover common callback shapes; keep callbacks readable and be explicit about captured state.

items.title: Generic collection interfaces
items.text: Select a collection from the operations the caller needs: order, key lookup, uniqueness, FIFO/LIFO, sorted access, concurrency, or immutability. Program against the narrowest useful interface and check equality/hash-code behavior for keys.

items.title: Reusable abstractions
items.text: For reusable abstractions, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to generic interfaces and delegates, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Type parameters across related APIs
items.text: Pick a parameter-passing form that communicates ownership and intent; avoid ref/out when a returned value is clearer.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates generic interfaces and delegates. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates generic interfaces and delegates rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for generic interfaces and delegates before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
